role.why: The classic test: the interviewer is not checking your pitch about the pen, but whether you ask questions before you sell. Starting with features is the wrong answer.
role.model: I would not start with the pen. I would ask first: “When did you last use a pen? What for? What happened the last time a pen let you down?” Say the answer is: “I sign contracts with clients every week, and last month my pen ran dry in front of a client.” Now I know the need (signing important documents), the pain (looking unprepared in front of a client) and what matters (reliability, image). Then I sell to that: “This pen is guaranteed for 2 years of writing and the refill shows how much ink is left, so you never run dry in front of a client again, and it looks like the pen of someone who closes deals.” And I close: “Shall I put two in your bag, one for the office and one for your meetings?” The structure is discovery, then a benefit tied to their words, then a clear ask. That is the same structure as a real B2B sale.

role.q: Walk me through your sales process, using a deal you closed.
role.why: Interviewers want to see a repeatable method with stages and numbers, not luck. A real example with figures makes it credible.
role.model: My process has six stages. 1. Prospecting: I target accounts that match our ideal customer profile. 2. Discovery: I understand their situation, their pain and its cost. 3. Qualification: budget, decision maker, timing, decision process. 4. Solution and demo: I show only what answers their pain. 5. Proposal and negotiation. 6. Closing and handover to onboarding. Example: a logistics company of 300 people that lost about 15 hours a week on manual order entry. I booked the first meeting with a cold e-mail that quoted their job ad for an order administrator. In discovery I put a figure on the pain: about €40,000 a year in time. I identified the operations director as the economic buyer and the IT manager as a technical gatekeeper, and ran a 2-week pilot with clear success criteria. The deal closed at €28,000 a year in 11 weeks, against an average cycle of 14 weeks, because the pilot criteria were agreed in writing before it started.

role.q: How do you prospect a new account?
role.why: Prospecting is most of the job for an SDR or a junior Account Executive. The interviewer checks that you target, research and follow up, instead of sending the same e-mail to everyone.
role.model: Three steps. First the target: I start from our ideal customer profile, for example French SaaS companies of 50 to 500 people that are hiring salespeople, and from the personas we sell to, here the Head of Sales and the Sales Ops manager. Second, research, 5 to 10 minutes per account: their website, recent news, job ads, the LinkedIn posts of the people I target, and a trigger that makes now a good time (fundraising, new manager, expansion). Third, a multichannel sequence over about three weeks: day 1 a short personalised e-mail with one trigger and one question, day 3 a call, day 5 a LinkedIn connection without a pitch, day 8 an e-mail with a useful case study, day 12 a call and voicemail, day 19 a polite break-up e-mail. Everything is logged in the CRM. I track the reply rate (aim for 5 to 10 %), the meetings booked and, above all, how many meetings become qualified opportunities, and I change the message that performs worst every two weeks.

role.q: The client says: “It’s too expensive.” What do you do?
role.why: The most common objection. A good answer neither drops the price straight away nor argues: it finds out what is really behind the objection.
role.model: I do not give a discount straight away: that teaches the client that the first price was not serious. First I acknowledge and ask: “I understand. Too expensive compared with what: your budget, another offer, or the value you expect?” The answer changes everything. If it is a budget problem, I look at the scope or the timing: a smaller first phase, or a start next quarter when the budget opens. If it is a competitor, I compare like for like: what is included, the cost of implementation, support. If it is value, I go back to the figures from discovery: “You told me this problem costs you about €60,000 a year; our solution is €18,000. Does that change the picture?” If I do negotiate, I always ask for something in return: a 2-year contract, a case study, a faster signature. And I check before moving on: “If we solve this point, is there anything else stopping you from signing?”

role.q: How do you qualify a lead? Do you know BANT or MEDDIC?
role.why: Qualification decides where you spend your time. The interviewer wants to see that you can say no to a bad deal early.
role.model: BANT is the simple version, useful for an SDR: Budget (is there money?), Authority (who decides?), Need (is there a real problem?), Timing (when?). For complex B2B deals I use MEDDIC: Metrics (the measurable gain the client expects, for example reduce churn by 2 points), Economic buyer (the person who can sign the budget), Decision criteria (what they will compare), Decision process (the steps: trial, legal, purchasing, signature), Identify pain (the problem and its cost) and Champion (someone inside who wants us to win and has influence). I write each point in the CRM with what I know and what is still missing. A deal with no economic buyer, no pain with a cost and no champion stays at the qualification stage, however enthusiastic the contact is. In my experience, disqualifying early is what keeps a win rate above 25 % instead of a pipeline full of deals that never close.

role.q: You are at 60 % of your quota with one month left. What do you do?
role.why: This tests how you handle pressure and whether you act on the pipeline with a plan, rather than hoping or giving everything away at a discount.
role.model: First I look at the facts, on day one. Say the quota is €300,000 and I am at €180,000: I need €120,000. I list every deal that could realistically close this month, with its amount, stage and next step, and I am honest about the probability. If I have, for example, €200,000 in late-stage deals, I need to close 60 % of them. Then I act on three fronts. 1. Late-stage deals: for each one, I confirm with the champion the exact signing steps (legal, purchasing, signature) and agree a mutual close plan with dates. 2. Speed things up with a reason, not just a discount: a start date that suits them, a limited offer approved by my manager, in exchange for signing this month. 3. Quick wins: upsells or renewals with existing clients who are happy. I tell my manager early, with the plan and the numbers, so they can help, for example by joining a call with an executive. And I keep prospecting a few hours a week, otherwise the next quarter starts empty.

role.q: How do you keep your CRM pipeline and your forecast reliable?
role.why: Managers live by the forecast. A salesperson whose forecast is reliable is trusted with bigger accounts.
role.model: Three habits. 1. Clear stage definitions based on what the client did, not on how I feel: for example “Proposal” only when the client has confirmed the budget and asked for the offer in writing. 2. Every deal always has a next step with a date, an amount and a close date that I update after each conversation; I review the whole pipeline every Friday for 30 minutes. 3. Clean-up: a deal with no activity for 30 days or a close date pushed back twice goes back a stage or is closed lost. For the forecast, I separate “commit” (I would bet on it: economic buyer confirmed, signing process known), “best case” and “pipeline”, and I compare my past forecasts with what really closed. If I usually close 80 % of my commit, I say so. I also watch pipeline coverage: about 3 times the quota for the quarter, adjusted to my real win rate. The goal is a forecast within 10 % of the result.

role.q: Tell me about a deal you lost and what you learned.
role.why: Everyone loses deals. The interviewer checks that you analyse the loss honestly and changed something in your method.
role.model: I use a short structure: the situation, what went wrong, what I changed. Situation: a €45,000 deal with a retail group, six months of work, a great relationship with the IT manager, who was my champion. We lost to a cheaper competitor at the last step. What went wrong: I never met the finance director, who was the real economic buyer. My champion was convinced, but he could not defend the return on investment in front of finance, and I had no figures written in the client’s own terms. What I learned and changed: now I ask early, in the second meeting: “Who else will be involved in the decision, and who signs the budget?” I ask my champion to introduce me to the economic buyer before the proposal, and I build the business case with the client’s own figures. Since then I write the decision process in the CRM for every deal over €20,000, and I have not lost a deal to a buyer I had never met.
